Factorize once, cross-validate many times

Source: R/kcv.R
kcv_prepare.Rd

kcv_prepare() does the expensive part of kcv() (building and factorizing the covariance matrix, which depends only on the locations, the variogram model and the trend) and returns it as an object. kcv_run() then computes the cross-validation for one fold scheme from it, at a fraction of the cost. kcv(...) is equivalent to kcv_run(kcv_prepare(...), ...).

Usage

kcv_prepare(formula, locations, data, model, beta = NULL, ...)

kcv_run(
  prepared,
  nfold,
  folds = NULL,
  buffer = NULL,
  targets = NULL,
  y = NULL,
  beta = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

Formula defining the response and the trend, e.g. log(zinc) ~ 1 or log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist). A matrix response, such as cbind(log(zinc), log(copper)) ~ 1 or a matrix column of data, cross-validates each column with the same model, trend and folds; see "Several responses" below.

locations

A formula giving the coordinates (e.g. ~x + y) when data is a data.frame, or an sf object or sp Spatial*DataFrame holding both the locations and the variables (then data is not used).

data

A data.frame, when locations is a formula.

model

A gstat variogram model (gstat::vgm()) with fixed parameters. Supported: Nug, Exp, Sph, Gau, Mat, Ste, Cir, Pen, Bes, Wav, Hol and nested sums of them, with optional 2D geometric anisotropy.

beta

Optional, for a prepared object made for simple kriging (with beta): new trend coefficients, a vector of length p or a p x T matrix as in kcv(). The factorization of simple kriging does not depend on them.

...

As in kcv().

prepared

A kcv_prepared object from kcv_prepare().

nfold

As in gstat::krige.cv(): missing or nrow(data) for leave-one-out; a single integer k < n for random k-fold assignment (drawn exactly as krige.cv() does, so the same seed gives the same folds); or a vector of length n of fold identifiers.

folds

Optional vector of length n of fold identifiers, as an alternative to a vector nfold. Giving both nfold and folds is an error.

buffer

Optional radius for buffered leave-one-out, in coordinate units (\(\ge 0\)). Each observation is predicted from the observations farther than buffer from it; see "Buffered leave-one-out" below. Cannot be combined with nfold or folds.

targets

Optional, with buffer: the observations to predict, as row numbers or a logical vector of length n. The hold-out sets are still formed from all observations. Useful to estimate buffered leave-one-out statistics from a sample of points when the radius is large. By default every observation is predicted.

y

Optional new responses, replacing those of the data given to kcv_prepare(): a numeric vector of length n (output as from a single response) or an n x T matrix (T responses, output with a response column), with rows in the order of that data. The locations, trend covariates and model are those of prepared. Missing or non-finite values are an error.

Value

kcv_prepare(): a kcv_prepared object. kcv_run(): the same output as kcv().

Details

The prepared object holds an \(n \times n\) matrix (\(8 n^2\) bytes) and can be saved with saveRDS().

kcv_run(prepared, y = ) cross-validates new responses at the same locations, with the trend matrix and model stored in prepared, without another factorization: for example, many fields simulated at the observation locations. See "Several responses" in kcv().

See also

kcv_engine_prepare() for a precomputed covariance matrix; vignette("fastkcv") for timings.

Examples

data(meuse, package = "sp")
v <- gstat::vgm(0.59, "Sph", 897, 0.05)
p <- kcv_prepare(log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist), ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
p
#> <kcv_prepared> universal kriging, n = 155, p = 2, 187.7 Kb
#> Estimated reciprocal condition number of C: 0.0051
loo <- kcv_run(p)
set.seed(1)
rmse_10fold <- replicate(5, sqrt(mean(kcv_run(p, nfold = 10)$residual^2)))
rmse_10fold
#> [1] 0.3876193 0.3918699 0.3886007 0.3739821 0.3781501
# Buffered leave-one-out at several radii from the same factorization.
sapply(c(0, 200, 400), function(r) kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, buffer = r))$rmse)
#> [1] 0.3771621 0.4349331 0.4640929

# New responses at the same locations: here 20 random permutations of
# the observations, cross-validated from the same factorization.
set.seed(2)
perm <- replicate(20, sample(log(meuse$zinc)))
cv_perm <- kcv_run(p, nfold = 10, y = perm)
summary(kcv_metrics(cv_perm)$rmse)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.7316  0.8015  0.8146  0.8090  0.8259  0.8700
